newsitem.title: PERU: Red Cross veteran at centre of Peru hostage siege.
newsitem.headline: Red Cross veteran at centre of Peru hostage siege.

text.p: Michel Minnig, a 10-year veteran with the Red Cross, has been thrust into the limelight as the intermediary between Peru's government and leftist guerrillas holding hundreds of hostages in Lima.

Minnig is a Swiss citizen who has served with the Red Cross in eight countries, including Iraq, Nicaragua, Lebanon, Kenya and the former Yugoslavia before moving to Peru in August this year as head of the Red Cross delegation here.
Minnig, who is single and studied political science in Lausanne and Geneva, joined the Red Cross in 1986.
The Swiss' heavily-accented but fluent Spanish has become a familiar sound on radio and television here as Minnig remains unflappable in the face of constant harrassment from journalists.

The intermediary role in the four-day old siege has forced Minnig to show his physical strength as well as mental agility. Initially, being the only official allowed inside the besieged compound, the wiry 44-year old found himself hauling tens of five-gallon (20-litre) water containers to the residence as part of the Red Cross' humanitarian operation.
Minnig was requested to carry out the intermediary role by both the Peruvian government and the rebels because of the neutral status of the agency, Red Cross officials said.

One official in Lima, who asked not to be named, said Minnig's presence created a "physical link ... in and out of the compound" that was "an important first step to opening up the premises and establishing communication links. It shows the barrier can be brought down."

Armed rebels from the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence late on Tuesday, capturing ministers, ambassadors and businessmen who were attending a diplomatic reception.
Many have been released, but the rebels still hold about 340 hostages and have not retracted a threat to kill hostages should their jailed comrades not be freed.
Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, however, has maintained a hard line with the Marxist guerrillas, flatly refusing to meet their demands and insisting they lay down their arms.
